concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Perceptual organization aims to represent visual content in terms of modular and disentangled elements that make subsequent processing easier.
concepts.content: Perceptual organization aims to represent visual content in terms of modular and disentangled elements that make subsequent processing easier. In this way, perceptual organization shares the same goal as visual representation learning, although the former deals more with discrete structures whereas the latter has focused mostly on continuous representations. These two fields evolved somewhat separately, with perceptual organization having its roots in psychology and representation learning coming more from machine learning, but these days the end result is converging in the form of vision systems that see the world in terms of objects, parts, relationships, layers, and many other useful structures.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding perceptual organization helps unify discrete and continuous visual representations, improving how vision systems interpret objects and relationships.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perceptual organization represents visual content with modular, disentangled elements.
- It shares goals with visual representation learning but focuses on discrete structures.
- Both fields converge in vision systems recognizing objects, parts, and relationships.

concepts.title: perceptual group
concepts.one_liner: A perceptual group is a particular kind of visual representation that groups primitive elements into meaningful structures like contours and objects.
concepts.content:
A particular kind of visual representation, the **perceptual group**, becomes the central object of interest; we will see what these are, how to find them, and how they are related to the representation learning algorithms from the last chapter.

First, what is a perceptual group? Look at the photo in @fig-perceptual_organization-perc_org_teaser and consider what you see. Not what raw pixel values you see, but what structures you see. What are some structures you can name?

(see figure: A few kinds of perceptual organization in the human visual system.)

What a camera sees is the raw RGB pixel values of the photo. But what your mind sees is rather different. You see contours and surfaces, objects and events.

Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as *groups of primitive elements*: a contour is a group of points that form a line, an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive whole, and so on. - Understanding them is key in vision and representation learning.

concepts.title: Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities.
concepts.content: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities. There is no single definition of what constitutes a coherent entity; it varies depending on the task. A segment could correspond to a nameable object, an image region made of a single material, or a physically distinct piece of geometry (see @fig-perceptual_organization-ambiguous_segmentation_example).

concepts.title: $K$-Means Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: $K$-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot and can segment by assigning each pixel to the cluster of its color value.
concepts.content:
$K$-means, which we covered in @sec-representation_learning, is one of the simplest and most useful clustering algorithms, so let's try it for segmentation.

$K$-means operates on a data matrix of $N$ datapoints by $M$ features per datapoint. Our first task is to convert the segmentation problem to that format. The simplest approach is to let each pixel be a datapoint and the pixel's color be its feature vector. For ease of visualization, we use the $ab$ color value as the two-dimensional (2D) feature per pixel. An image represented this way can be plotted as a scatter plot and can be thought of as samples from a distribution over $ab$ colors, as shown in @fig-perceptual_organization-scatter_ab_fruits2.

(see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...)

$K$-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot (and, if you prefer a probabilistic interpretation, it can be thought of as fitting a mixture of Gaussians to the datapoints, which aims to approximate the distribution from which these pixels were sampled). We can segment via $k$-means by simply assigning each pixel to the cluster assignment of its color value. Below we color each pixel in each cluster by the mean color of all pixels assigned to that cluster (@fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_ab_fruits2).

(see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.)

Naturally, $k$-means on $ab$-values finds segments that correspond to regions of roughly a constant color. This simple approach can be surprisingly effective. Notice how it segments a zebra from the background in @fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_ab_zebra_and_beach (because the black and white stripes have roughly the same $ab$-values). However, it fails to group more complex patterns that are not defined by color similarity, as in the beach photo in @fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_ab_zebra_and_beach.
concepts.motivation_md: $K$-means segmentation converts image pixels into feature vectors and clusters them by color, enabling simple and effective segmentation of regions with similar colors.
concepts.recap_md:
- $K$-means clusters pixels by their $ab$ color values.
- Each pixel is assigned to the cluster of its color.
- Effective for segmenting regions of roughly constant color.

concepts.title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation models a distance metric (affinity) that tells us whether two items should be grouped.
concepts.content:
Other clustering methods are based on the idea of affinity, where we try to model a distance metric (the affinity) that tells us whether two items should be grouped. The distance metric usually measures how similar two patterns are, or how likely they are to be part of the same object.

For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between the color values of the two pixels. There are numerous ways to use such an affinity to group pixels into segments, all sharing the general idea that pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group and pixels with low affinity should belong to different groups. Methods using this idea include those based on graph cuts @shi2000normalized, spectral clustering @arbelaez2010contour, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering (@sec-probabilistic_graphical_models).

We do not have time to cover all these methods and in fact they are no longer commonly used. Instead, we focus on a method seen earlier in the book that is in common use: contrastive learning (covered in @sec-representation_learning-contrastive_learning). Contrastive learning fits affinity-based segmentation because it learns from similarities (positive pairs) and differences (negative pairs), which is what an affinity metric provides! Contrastive methods learn an embedding where datapoints with high affinity are nearby and those with low affinity are far apart. Once we have such an embedding, clustering is easy in the embedding space, and almost any off-the-shelf clustering algorithm will work; for simplicity, we use $k$-means in this book.

In this book, we present one way to do affinity-based clustering: first use affinities to supervise an embedding in which the data is nearly clustered, then read off the clusters using a simple quantization method like $k$-means. There are many other affinity-based methods but this simple method often works well.

If we define affinities in terms of color distance, then there's no point in learning such an embedding, because the raw colors themselves are already a great embedding under that notion of affinity. Affinity-based clustering becomes interesting when we have nontrivial affinities to model; for example, given by human judgments about which pixels should go together in natural images.

Because human supervision is expensive and limiting, a popular alternative is to use self-supervised affinity measures, just like in self-supervised contrastive learning. Popular contrastive learning methods like SimCLR @chen2020simple, MoCo @he2020momentum, and DINO @caron2021emerging train a mapping from image patches to embedding vectors such that two patches from the same image embed near each other and patches from different images embed far apart. We can run these methods densely (in a sliding window fashion) across a single image to create a feature map of size $C \times N \times M$, where $N$ and $M$ are spatial dimensions and $C$ is the embedding dimensionality. This creates a new image where each pixel has a value (the embedding vector) similar to other pixels the model thinks would likely appear in the same scene. Effectively, we have learned an affinity metric based on natural patch co-occurrences, then used that affinity metric to obtain a feature map revealing coherent image regions. Applying $k$-means to pixels in this feature map yields effective segmentation. This pipeline is shown in @fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_dino, using DINO @caron2021emerging as the contrastive embedding.
concepts.motivation_md: Affinity-based segmentation models similarity between pixels to group them, enabling segmentation beyond simple color similarity by learning embeddings that reflect complex affinities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Affinity models a distance metric indicating if items should be grouped.
- Contrastive learning can learn embeddings reflecting affinities.
- Clustering such embeddings (e.g., with $k$-means) yields segmentation.

concepts.title: edge detection
concepts.one_liner: Edges in an image form a good, compact representation of the image's content because they are relatively sparse and stable to noise and lighting.
concepts.content: Edge detection is based on the idea that edges in an image should form a good, compact representation of the image's content because edges are relatively sparse and stable with respect to nuisances like noise and lighting. Subsequent work identified connections between different kinds of edge structure and scene geometry; for example, an edge that represents an occluding contour indicates a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Edge detection captures important structural information in images by identifying boundaries that are stable and sparse, aiding in understanding scene geometry.
concepts.recap_md:

- Edges are sparse and stable to noise and lighting.
- Some edges correspond to depth discontinuities in scenes.

concepts.title: layer
concepts.one_liner: Layers represent different planes in a scene, such as sky, mountains, trees, and foreground characters, which can be shifted to create parallax.
concepts.content: For example, on the back plane would be the sky, then there would be mountains on the next plane, then trees, and then the foreground characters. During filming, the planes could be shifted back and forth to create parallax where the foreground planes move more quickly than the planes further back.
concepts.motivation_md: Layer representations help model depth and motion effects like parallax by organizing scene elements into separate planes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Layers represent different depth planes in a scene.
- Examples include sky, mountains, trees, and foreground.
- Shifting layers creates parallax effects in filming.
